abstract_sentences.text: Instructed code editing, where LLMs directly modify a developer’s existing code based on a user instruction, is becoming a widely used interaction mode in AI coding assistants.

evidence.anchor: directly modify a developer’s existing code

abstract_sentences.text: However, few benchmarks directly evaluate this capability and current datasets often rely on artificial sources.

evidence.anchor: few benchmarks directly evaluate this capability

abstract_sentences.text: We introduce EDIT-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM code editing capabilities grounded in real-world usage, i.e., user instructions and code contexts collected in the wild.

evidence.anchor: user instructions and code contexts collected in the wild

abstract_sentences.text: EDIT-Bench comprises of 540 problems, multiple natural and programming languages, and a diverse set of real-world use cases, ranging from resolving errors to adding features.
EDIT-Bench introduces context-dependent problems that require the model to understand code context, highlighted code, and cursor position in addition to the user instruction.
We evaluate 40 diverse LLMs and observe that EDIT-Bench is a challenging set of problems where only 1 model scores over 60%.
We find that model performance varies across different categories of user instructions.
Further, we find that different levels of contextual information greatly affect task success rate, with performance varying up to 8%, indicating the importance of evaluating with realistic context.

experimental_design.name: collection source
experimental_design.description: An open-source VSCode extension mimics Copilot/Cursor instructed editing; the extension records instructions, code context, responses, and accepted-edit status.

evidence.anchor: VS Code extension that mimics existing instructed code editing tools

experimental_design.name: raw user sample
experimental_design.description: The paper reports 458 users and 2,672 accepted-edit responses, described in the introduction as nearly 500 users.

experimental_design.name: privacy and IRB
experimental_design.description: Privacy settings govern logging of instruction, prefix/suffix, highlight, cursor, code context, and responses; the data collection process was IRB approved.

evidence.anchor: reviewed and approved by our institution’s IRB

experimental_design.name: curation filter
experimental_design.description: The authors focus on Python/Javascript responses, remove similar prompts, and remove trivial, stylistic, or ambiguous tasks, leaving around 470 interesting/challenging problems.

evidence.anchor: filtering process left us with around 470 problems

experimental_design.name: benchmark composition
experimental_design.description: The paper reports 540 problems, five natural languages, two programming languages, 74 unique imports, and four functional edit clusters.

experimental_design.name: category distribution
experimental_design.description: Feature addition, feature modification, bug fixing, and optimization account for 43%, 27%, 22%, and 8% respectively.

experimental_design.name: model panel
experimental_design.description: Forty models span GPT, Qwen, Llama, Mistral, Sonnet, Gemma, Grok, Deepseek, Gemini, Kimi, and GLM families; the family counts sum to 40.

experimental_design.name: provider and reasoning setup
experimental_design.description: GPT models use OpenAI API, Claude uses Anthropic API, and other models use OpenRouter; default settings are used, temperature is 0 when possible, and GPT reasoning variants use medium/high effort.

experimental_design.name: primary metric
experimental_design.description: Pass@1 uses one generated code sample per problem and counts a problem solved only when all unit tests pass.

evidence.anchor: 1 code sample is generated per problem

experimental_design.name: easy/hard rule
experimental_design.description: Hard tasks are solved by k or fewer models and Easy tasks are the remainder; k=20 is selected for an approximately even split.

experimental_design.name: prompt variants
experimental_design.description: Whole equals +Highlight, Cursor Position equals +Highlight + Cursor, and No Highlight removes highlighted-code information; main experiments use +Highlight only.

evidence.anchor: models perform best when given highlighted code

experimental_design.name: execution environment
experimental_design.description: Evaluations run inside an Ubuntu 22.04 Docker container; a release Dockerfile is promised but no image or build digest appears in the paper.

experimental_design.name: random seeds and repetitions
experimental_design.description: No random seed, per-model repeat count, stochastic sample aggregation, or seed-level uncertainty is reported; temperature 0 is used only when possible.

experimental_design.name: leakage and contamination controls
experimental_design.description: The paper gives no train/test split protocol for translated pairs, hidden-test coverage, contamination rate, or held-out freshness experiment; Appendix F discusses documentation and continuous releases instead.

result_inventory.claim: EditBench has a more in-the-wild and context-rich benchmark profile than the listed edit datasets.
result_inventory.value: 540 problems; 5 NL; 2 PL; instruction 238 ± 738; code context 5642 ± 7567; HL=Yes; 74 unique Python imports.
result_inventory.comparison: CanItEdit 105, EditEval 194, Aider Polyglot 225; their sources are annotator or coding-exercise based and HL=No; imports are 25, 16, and 15.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Descriptive benchmark-level comparison; Table 1 states ± is standard deviation; no inferential test or task denominator beyond reported counts.

result_inventory.value: Feature addition 43%; feature modification 27%; bug fixing 22%; optimization 8%.
result_inventory.comparison: All four categories sum to the reported benchmark distribution.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Descriptive category proportions; category sample counts and uncertainty are not given.

result_inventory.claim: The benchmark is difficult for the evaluated model panel.
result_inventory.value: claude-sonnet-4 pass@1 = 66.67%; only 1 of 40 models exceeds 60%.
result_inventory.comparison: Figure 4 ranks all 40 open and closed models.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Per-problem pass@1 with one sample; cross-task aggregation is reported descriptively with no interval or significance test.

result_inventory.claim: Easy and hard questions differ sharply.
result_inventory.value: Average gap across models = 59.3%, SD = 10.6%; hard instructions are nearly five times shorter and highlighted code is slightly longer.
result_inventory.comparison: Easy versus Hard split uses k=20; Appendix Table 8 gives instruction 351.21 ± 1018.87 versus 75.09 ± 107.20 and highlight 942.30 ± 1275.35 versus 881.45 ± 1275.23.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Model-level average gap and descriptive character-length means; no test or group denominator is given.

result_inventory.claim: Highlighted code tends to help while cursor position has mixed effects.
result_inventory.value: Adding highlight improves 5/7 models; relative changes versus Code Only are +2.40, +2.78, +0.37, +1.85, +3.52, -3.15, and -2.59. +Highlight + Cursor is also mixed.
result_inventory.comparison: Seven top models from different families are evaluated under Code Only, +Highlight, +Cursor, and +Highlight + Cursor.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Pass@1 in a prompt ablation; no paired test, uncertainty, or multiplicity correction.

evidence.anchor: Highlighted code is crucial to performance

result_inventory.claim: Closed models rank higher overall, although open models include strong examples.
result_inventory.value: Only 4 of top 15 are open and bottom 15 are all open; glm-4.6 is best open at 56.48%, with kimi-k2 and deepseek-chat-v3.1 close.
result_inventory.comparison: Figure 4 color-codes Closed and Open; gpt-5 medium is below gpt-5-mini.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Descriptive rank and access-group comparison; no access-matched test or inferential model.

evidence.anchor: only 4 out of the top 15 are open models

result_inventory.claim: Edit category changes model performance and model-specific strengths.
result_inventory.value: Average bug fixing = 52.2%; optimization = 44.6%; feature addition = 39.6%; claude-sonnet-4 ranks first except optimization.
result_inventory.comparison: Figure 5 shows qwen3-coder-flash strongest on bug fixing and claude-sonnet-4 strongest on feature modification.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Category pass@1 averages; category sample counts, dispersion, and tests are absent.

evidence.anchor: different models perform best at different categories

result_inventory.claim: EditBench has weak positive associations with maintained comparison leaderboards.
result_inventory.value: Aider Polyglot shared n=17: Pearson r=0.24, p=0.06; Chatbot Arena coding shared n=30: r=0.11, p=0.01.
result_inventory.comparison: The comparison is to Aider Polyglot and the coding subset of Chatbot Arena, not to a matched task-level benchmark.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Pearson correlation with reported p values; no interval, robust correlation, multiplicity correction, or test identity.

result_inventory.claim: Average pass@1 falls across longer context bins.
result_inventory.comparison: Appendix E bins context by character length.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Descriptive average pass@1 with unspecified ± level; no covariate adjustment or length-effect test.

evidence.anchor: models tend to do better on shorter context length problems

result_inventory.claim: Easy and hard instruction lengths differ more than highlight lengths.
result_inventory.value: Easy instruction = 351.21 ± 1018.87 versus Hard = 75.09 ± 107.20; Easy highlight = 942.30 ± 1275.35 versus Hard = 881.45 ± 1275.23.
result_inventory.comparison: Easy and Hard use the k=20 difficulty rule.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Descriptive character-length means and ± values; no denominator or inferential comparison.

result_inventory.claim: Most sampled user votes selected at least one response.
result_inventory.value: Left 50.8%; right 34.6%; neither 14.6%; at least one accepted 85.4%.
result_inventory.comparison: Left/right/neither vote categories in EditBenchExt data analysis.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Descriptive vote proportions; no user weighting, repeat-user handling, or uncertainty.

final_judgment.single_storyline: The paper turns IDE interactions containing instruction, full code, highlight, and cursor into human-reviewed executable harnesses, then uses 40-model pass@1, context variants, and edit categories to expose real-world instructed-edit difficulty (pp.2-8).
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The main body keeps the collection motivation, curation and harness overview, benchmark scope, dataset comparisons, overall model ranking, context/category results, leaderboard correlations, and the concise conclusion (pp.3-9).
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Appendix A-F moves prompt text, privacy operations, distributions, full examples, provider links, extra context analyses, automatic-harness failure, contamination, and broader impact to pp.14-27; reproducibility and negative-result interpretation therefore require the appendix.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Figure 1 establishes the four-part interaction input, Table 1 makes benchmark source/context differences scannable, Figure 4 gives overall ranking, and Table 3 plus Figure 5 split the headline into context and category mechanisms (pp.2,5,7-8).
final_judgment.largest_gap: The PDF leaves 109 core versus 104+9 tested counts, Portuguese versus Polish, and 540 versus catalog 545 unresolved; the evaluation also omits seeds, intervals, task denominators, test identities, and harness validation, so generality and harness quality are only partly closed (pp.4-8,22,26-27).
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For in-the-wild code-edit benchmarks, preserve the interaction context visible at request time and convert it into executable, generalizable tests with independent review before comparing models (pp.3-4,23-25).
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This rule fits single-file instructed edits evaluated by unit-test pass@1; the paper does not establish multi-file agentic issue resolution, fully automatic harness generation, unrepresented programming languages, or every IDE workflow (pp.3,6,22,27).
